1:
Where the chapter stands in the letter is agreed. Chrysostom has the Apostle, having finished his discourse of almsgiving and shown that he loves more than he is loved, now opportunely entering on points that involve more of reproof, with allusion to the false apostles. Calvin says he proceeds partly to refute the calumnies with which he had been defamed and partly to repress the insolence of persons who could not bear restraint, both having construed his vehemence to the destruction of his authority. Robertson calls it the third part of the epistle, in which he vigorously defends himself against a stubborn minority, adding that great ministers have passed through such trials ever since. Gill says simply that he returns to the vindication of himself.

What tone he takes in doing it is not agreed at all. Henry hears mildness: he addresses them in a very mild and humble manner and is plainly desirous that no occasion be given him to use severity, and where at the opening of the letter he had joined another with himself he now speaks only for himself. Wesley hears the same, that he entreats after the meekness and gentleness of Christ though he might have commanded, and takes the emphatic I Paul myself for an answer to the charge that he was base when present. Ellicott hears the opposite. The Apostle's thoughts have travelled back to Corinth and the stinging words reported to him vex his soul, so that he speaks in a tone of suppressed indignation showing itself in keen incisive irony, the opening formula being one he reserves for exceptionally strong emotion. At the next verse he is blunter: there is an implied warning, almost a menace, in the entreaty, and if the necessity for boldness comes it will be the worse for them.

Two things at that verse are noticed by one man each. Calvin reports that some think the discourse incomplete, the request never being expressed, and is rather of opinion that what was wanting in the former clause is completed here. Robertson notices that the verb has changed between the verses and suggests that I beg suits the new turn. Clarke reconstructs the charge itself, that it is customary for cowards and overbearing men to threaten the weak when present, to bluster when absent and to be obsequious before the strong, and that this was laid to the Apostle's account.

The distinction he then draws is where the argument begins. Robertson puts it most sharply: walking in the flesh is a very different thing from walking by the standards of the flesh, which is what his enemies charged, and it is easy enough to make insinuations. Ellicott gives the usage, that the first phrase generally means the simple fact of bodily existence with all its incidental infirmities and trials and commonly implies no sin, where the second does. Gill concedes the first and denies the second: they were in the body, in a state of imperfection, attended with weaknesses and surrounded with afflictions, and in that sense walked in the flesh. Barnes says the Apostle claimed no exemption from the common wants and frailties of nature. Calvin calls it a concession of no service to his adversaries, since being shut up in the prison of his body did not prevent the Spirit from showing itself marvellously in his weakness. Clarke turns the denial into defiance: he does not act the coward as they insinuate, having a good cause, a good captain, strength at will and courage at hand, and fearing neither them nor their master. Wesley and Robertson both note the plural, Wesley adding that it is used for modesty and decency though the Apostle principally means himself.
4:
Gill alone restricts the warfare: it is not that common to all believers, enlisted under the captain of their salvation, but what is peculiar to ministers of the gospel, the ministerial office and its discharge. Everyone else leaves it general. Clarke notes that the metaphor of a campaign is often used of the life and trials of a minister, and identifies the carnal weapons with what the opposing party actually did — calumniating him, traducing the truth, preaching licentious doctrine. Ellicott says the phrase is essentially military, pointing to its use in the Greek version for the capture of fortresses, and takes the weapons for the energies of spiritual powers given by the Eternal Spirit. Barnes lists what they are not: neither eloquence nor talent nor learning nor wealth nor any external advantage men rely on to advance a cause. Wesley narrows the armoury, granting that faith and prayer belong to it but judging the word of God chiefly intended. Calvin observes that the warfare corresponds to the weapons, the character of one following from the other by an argument from contraries. Robertson alone reports a textual point, that the noun is campaign and not army as some copies have it, though both forms turn up in the papyri.

What is cast down is read four ways. Barnes takes the word in the sense of device and refers it to the plans of a wicked world, particularly the systems of false philosophy, so entrenched that they might be called the stronghold of God's enemies. Clarke goes at those systems directly: the Greek philosophers valued themselves on ethical schemes whose reasoning appeared profound and conclusive, but were obliged to assume principles that either did not exist or were false, as their whole mythology evidently was. Gill keeps it to the carnal reasonings of natural men against God and against every truth of the gospel, all disproved and silenced by the preaching of the word. Ellicott makes the sharpest connection: the noun is formed from the very verb used two verses earlier of what his opponents reckoned about him, so it would be better to carry the continuity over and render it thoughts, or reckonings. Robertson keeps the siege in view, the reasonings being forts to be taken. Wesley presses the next phrase, that the thought brought into captivity is rather the faculty of the mind, which being overcome lays down all authority of its own. Calvin reads a change of subject, from the conflict with what rises in opposition to the ordinary preparation by which men are brought into subjection, since so long as we rest in our own judgment we are not subject at all.

What the threatened vengeance amounts to divides them by instrument. Gill takes it not of the temporal sword but the spiritual — censures and excommunication, used with the suffrage of the church to reclaim the disobedient, or rather the extraordinary power an apostle held. Wesley includes both, spiritual censure and miraculous punishment. Calvin says the power was given not merely to constrain voluntary disciples but to inflict something on the rebellious. Barnes keeps the chapter's contrast in view, that though his weapons are not carnal and though he is modest when present, he is prepared to act. Robertson glosses the terms, the idiom for readiness being found in the historians and the word for disobedience a rare one meaning to hear amiss, a refusal to heed. On why it waits, Clarke says until they have wholly discountenanced these men and separated from their communion, the Apostle being in no haste. Wesley gives the reason nobody else gives: until the sound part of them have given proof of obedience, so that he is in no danger of punishing the innocent with the guilty. Ellicott hears the same qualification in the text, the words that follow implying that the opening ones were too unqualified.
7:
The opening clause can be read several ways, and Calvin sets them all out before choosing: the phrase may mean the reality itself or an outward mask that deceives us; the sentence may be interrogative or affirmative; the verb imperative or indicative. Ellicott reduces the field to three and settles it — indicative, imperative and interrogative are all possible, but ye look on things gives the most satisfactory sense. Robertson agrees in a line: either mood makes sense, but the indicative best, and they ought to look below the surface. Gill hears irony and a reproof for judging by appearance, and alone lists what they judged by — the meanness of his person, the weakness of his body, the lowness of his voice, his poverty. Henry puts the question back: is outward appearance a fit measure to judge persons by, and to judge between him and his adversaries? Barnes says the same of the other side, that his rivals valued themselves on external advantages and claimed peculiar honour because they were superior in personal appearance. Clarke narrows the indefinite pronoun to one man, the false apostle who had made so much disturbance in the church. Wesley leaves the man to his own reflection, before a severer method convinces him.

Chrysostom stands back to admire the management: what one may especially admire in Paul is that, having fallen on an urgent necessity for exalting himself, he contrives both to do it and not to appear offensive on account of the egotism, as may be seen particularly in the letter to the Galatians.

The boast that follows is qualified differently by each. Ellicott makes a suggestion nobody else makes, that the word rendered somewhat more is literally somewhat too much and may be quoted from a term his critics had used; and he holds it scarcely questionable that the authority claimed includes power to enforce itself by supernatural chastisement. Gill measures it against the field: to claim greater authority than the false apostles, or even than true ministers in common, would still not exceed the bounds of truth and modesty. Calvin finds the modesty in the earlier plural, by which he put himself among those he greatly excelled, though not so as to leave his authority impaired. Clarke turns the verse into a rule of office, quoting a maxim that this is what pastors ever propose to themselves in exercising authority, employing it for edification and not for the destruction of any delinquent. Robertson glosses the closing verb: he will not be put to shame as a convicted impostor or pretentious boaster.

Everyone agrees the next sentence is broken, and each supplies it his own way. Gill says plainly that something is wanting and fills it with a refusal: though he might lawfully boast of the apostles' authority over the insolent, he forbears it and drops the subject. Clarke calls it elliptical and supplies another clause, that he has not used this authority and will add no more, lest he seem, as his adversary insinuated, to wish to terrify them by letters. Barnes supplies the connection, that he says he might boast more so as not to appear to terrify them with letters merely, since he does not threaten more than he can perform. Ellicott makes the suppressed clause the substance of the threat, that the sentence he might pass will be no hollow form, so that he may not seem to frighten them as with a bugbear. Wesley reduces it to five words, threatening more than I can perform. Calvin gives the taunt in the opponents' mouths: what does he mean by terrifying them with letters at a distance when he is another thing in their presence? Robertson notes that the word for frightening occurs nowhere else in the New Testament though it is common in the Greek Old Testament; he and Ellicott both notice that letters stands in the plural.
10:
Ellicott marks what is singular here: allusive references to what was said of the Apostle at Corinth have appeared often already, but here for the first time we have the very words quoted, and the scorn in them had wounded his sensitive nature like a poisoned arrow. Whether one man or a party said them is disputed, and two voices reach the same answer by different roads. Robertson reports the manuscripts: the older Latin gives they say, but the critical editors prefer a singular, says one. Gill gets there from the versions, the Syriac and the Latin both pointing the same way, and thinks one particular person is in view whom the Apostle does not choose to name. Robertson adds an ambiguity nobody else raises: the two adjectives can be uncomplimentary, meaning severe and violent rather than impressive and vigorous. Clarke fills out the sneer, that when you behold the man you find him a feeble and contemptible mortal, and when you hear him his doctrine is good for nothing. Wesley passes on the tradition an early father gives for the bodily weakness, that his stature was low, his body crooked and his head bald.

The reply is read as a threat by three and as something else by one. Barnes has him contradicting the charge outright, so that none should flatter themselves there would be any discrepancy between his words and his deeds. Clarke thinks the threat told: it would doubtless have alarmed the false apostle, who very likely did not await the coming, being unwilling to try the fate of Elymas. Robertson keeps to the pronoun, which asks not what nor who but what sort, so that his quality in his letters when absent and in his deeds when present is precisely the same. Ellicott changes the tense and with it the force: since a verb must be supplied it is better to supply the present, such are we, making the sentence less a threat of a particular instance than a statement of the settled character of his life.

On the self-measuring at the end, five of them read the disclaimer as irony. Gill reports that some take it so, as though he would not pretend to put himself on a level with men of such gifts and learning and eloquence. Barnes calls it a strain of severe but delicate irony, in which the man accused of wanting boldness says he is not bold enough to do what they had done. Wesley calls it a strong irony and glosses the two verbs, to equal themselves as partners of the same office and to compare themselves as partakers of the same labour. Clarke puts the substance plainly, that he dares neither associate with nor compare himself to those who are full of self-commendation. Calvin extends the stroke, since he afterwards does not merely compare himself boldly with them but, deriding their vanity, leaves them far behind — and the blow falls not only on the boasters but on the Corinthians, who encouraged them by a misdirected approbation.

What is wrong with the method is put four ways. Henry says they took a wrong course in measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves among themselves, which was not wise, since they prided themselves on their own attainments. Clarke gives the reason: they are not sent of God nor inspired by his Spirit, and therefore have no rule to think or act by. Wesley sees them choosing and limiting their provinces according to their own fancy. Ellicott and Robertson both hear a play on the two verbs, one meaning to number among and the other to compare, the sound of the first suggesting the second; and Ellicott adds the translator's complaint, that the half-playful assonance is hard to convey in English.
13:
What the measure is gets four different answers. Robertson takes the word itself, an old term for a reed or measuring rod, common in the papyri and the ancestor of our word canon, which occurs only twice in the New Testament. Wesley makes it a providential allotment, God having assigned each apostle his province and its bounds, and this one the province of the Gentiles. Gill says the same more briefly, that they did not go beyond the bounds set by God's providence in coming to Corinth. Ellicott alone gives it a documentary sense: the measure is the concordat established between this Apostle and Barnabas on the one side and Peter, James and John on the other, whose terms he had not transgressed. Clarke turns it into a map: they had not gone straight from Macedonia through Thessaly and across the Adriatic into Italy, which would have carried them past Corinth westward, but had left that direct path and come south through Greece into Achaia, planting the gospel there. Calvin puts the contrast rather than the definition, setting the Apostle's moderation against the presumption of the false apostles and finding the true measure of glorying in keeping within one's limits.

Two of them warn that the text here is unsafe. Clarke says there is great difficulty in this verse and the three that follow, the manuscripts differing so that the true reading can scarcely be determined, our own version being perhaps the plainest that can be made of it. Barnes finds the obscurity in the brevity rather than the copies, and reports an older English rendering, that we will not rejoice above measure. Ellicott supplies the particular variant the others only gesture at: some of the better manuscripts omit the negative, and on that reading the sentence becomes a question — are we over-reaching, as though you were not within the limit assigned to us? Robertson adds that the double compound verb for stretching too far seems to have been made by the Apostle himself, turning up afterwards only in one late father. Calvin describes the gesture behind it, of men who stretch out their arms or raise themselves on their feet to catch at what is not within reach.

Who was accused of reaping another man's harvest is the last question, and Ellicott alone treats it as a counter-charge. The words, he says, are not merely defensive: the Apostle presses the charge of intrusion home, since it was they and not he who found ground for their boasts in other men's labours — though the context leads to the conclusion that the charge was first brought against him, they having spoken of him as pushing into ground that was not his. Calvin says the same without the reversal, that the false apostles, having put their hand to another man's harvest, had the audacity to revile the men who had prepared a place for them at the cost of sweat and toil. Barnes gives the sequence plainly, that they came after he had been there and entered into his labours; Robertson reduces it to four words, that he founded the church at Corinth. Clarke answers in the language of the games, that they never attempted to enter into other men's labours but study to convert the regions assigned them by the Spirit, entering the course lawfully and running according to rule. Gill notes that the disclaimer is repeated so that it may be explained.

On what is hoped from their growth the two who take it up agree. Wesley reads it practically: their faith being increased they can the better spare him, and the enlargement is their enabling him to go further still. Robertson keeps to the grammar, noting the genitive absolute in the growing of their faith.
16:
Where the regions beyond lie is guessed at by three and settled by one. Barnes says frankly that it can only be matter of conjecture, offers other parts of Greece — Arcadia, perhaps, or Lacedaemon — and passes on another man's suggestion that since the Corinthians were engaged in commerce the Apostle hoped the gospel might travel by their trade. Clarke looks south to the Morea and Sparta and west to Italy, adding that he does not appear to have reckoned Libya or any part of Africa within his province. Wesley says only that it means westward and southward, where the gospel had not yet been preached, and Gill that he hoped providence would direct him into the more remote parts. Ellicott alone settles it from the Apostle's own later words, which make it clear that he is thinking of western Greece, of Rome, and chiefly of Spain — where, he adds, the gospel could be preached without even the risk of its being said that he was building on another man's foundation, which is the whole point of the passage. Robertson contributes the word, a compound adverb meaning beyond those places, used here as a preposition and found nowhere else outside the ecclesiastical writers.

The maxim that follows is treated as a correction. Calvin says it is added because the glorying just claimed might have the appearance of empty boasting, so that the Apostle cites himself and his rivals alike before the judgment-seat of God, where those glory on good grounds who are approved there. Barnes concedes that boasting is not always improper, since this Apostle boasts elsewhere, only never of his own power or attainments. Clarke makes the rule turn on the source of success: none can succeed without the especial blessing of God, so let God who gave the blessing have the glory, and even a man commissioned immediately from God takes no praise to himself. Gill enumerates what is excluded — not himself, nor his outward circumstances, nor his inward endowments, nor his natural or acquired parts, nor wisdom or knowledge or learning or eloquence, nor his own righteousness and labours, and much less other men's. Ellicott turns aside to complain of the translators, who have yielded again to their besetting weakness for variation by rendering the same verb two ways. Robertson disposes of the verse in five words, noting only that the Apostle is quoting.

What self-commendation amounts to is then described from four sides. Gill defines it as ascribing to oneself what does not belong to one — claiming to be a minister of Christ and sent by him when one is not, or boasting of large ministerial gifts when one has none. Clarke draws the portrait: the man who makes a parade of his own attainments, who preaches himself and not Christ Jesus the Lord, and who so far from being a servant for Christ's sake affects to be a ruler. Barnes states the principle instead, that a man is not to be judged by the estimate he places on himself but by the estimate God forms and expresses, and that a readiness to commend oneself is no evidence at all of being saved. Robertson glosses the word for approved as accepted, and adds that it is the Lord's own recommendation that is accepted. Calvin closes on the practical difficulty, that it is easy to impose on men by a false impression and happens every day, so that we should leave off everything else and aim exclusively at being approved by God, satisfied with his approbation alone, which ought justly to be reckoned of more value than all the applause there is. Ellicott makes one last observation about the chapter as a whole: here again, as at the twelfth verse and in five passages before it, we can trace the impression which the stinging taunt had left on the Apostle's mind.
